newsitem.title: PERU: MRTA defeat a blow to LatAm rebels' thinning ranks.
newsitem.headline: MRTA defeat a blow to LatAm rebels' thinning ranks.

text.p: The swift and brutal raid by Peruvian commandos that killed 14 Tupac Amaru guerrillas holding 72 hostages in Lima was a serious psychological blow to the thinning ranks of leftist insurgents in Latin America, analysts said.

While Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) still has firepower, with perhaps 200 rebels hiding in the jungle, its political leadership and inspiration were lost in Tuesday's spectacular attack on the Japanese envoy's residence.

"The MRTA is now without political leadership," said historian Nelson Manrique of Lima's Catholic University, adding that siege leader Nestor Cerpa was "the last MRTA political leader still free. The rest are inexperienced youngsters."
"I don't believe the MRTA can regroup, at least in the short term," said Peruvian guerrilla expert Carlos Tapia.

That leaves a seriously weaker guerrilla threat in one of the only two Latin American countries with an active guerrilla war, the other being Colombia. Mexico's two Marxist rebel groups are under a ceasefire or trying to restart peace talks.

The apparent ease with which the MRTA were overpowered and all but one of the hostages freed shows that Latin American rebels are not what they were a few decades ago, when they could pose serious threats even to the most brutal military regimes.
But only two of the innumerable leftist uprisings in Latin America ever achieved their main objective -- Fidel Castro's Cuban revolution in 1959 and the Sandinistas in Nicaragua 20 years later.
Castro has been in power nearly 40 years. The Sandinistas were beaten in democratic elections in 1990 and 1996.

Castro's triumph, and his Argentine-born lieutenant Ernesto "Che" Guevara's call to arms to create "one, 10, 100 Vietnams in Latin America," gave ideological inspiration to guerrilla groups up and down the region.

But they met determined foes in Venezuela's civilian government of the early 1960s and the military dictatorships of Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Uruguay in the 1970s, and lost their following to democratic reforms that have swept the region.

Some were beaten, such as Uruguay's Tupamaros, one of the earliest rebel groups, born in 1960 but vanquished by 1972, Argentina's Montoneros and ERP, which succumbed to a brutal military crackdown in the mid-1970s, and Ecuador's colourfully named Afaro Vive, Carajo!, defeated in the 1980s.

Others signed peace deals and became involved in mainstream politics -- Colombia's M-19, which made spectacular attacks in the 1980s; El Salvador's Farabundo Marti rebels; and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit, which signed a treaty last year after a three-decade struggle that was Latin America's longest.

But in Peru, the Maoist-inspired Shining Path, bigger and bloodier than the MRTA despite being overshadowed during the Lima siege, has notched up 1,484 guerrilla attacks and an estimated 27,000 deaths.

Since President Alberto Fujimori's government captured its leader Abimael Guzman in 1992, the Shining Path has been a pale reflection of the group that 10 years ago sowed terror in the countryside and periodically paralysed Lima with its "armed strikes."

The hardiest survivors are probably the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), born in 1964 and waging war on the state ever since, apart from a brief truce with President Belisario Bentacur in 1984.
They have resisted recent peace overtures from Colombia's current President Ernesto Samper, and have been holding dozens of soldiers for eight months in Latin America's "other" hostage crisis.
